title: First aid
description: A longitudinal first-aid programme from spotting danger and calling for help (ages 3-5) to primary assessment, CPR knowledge and emergency simulations (12-17). The app teaches knowledge only: hands-on skills need an accredited course with a qualified instructor. Do not become the second victim.

competencies.title: Can recognise danger and stay safe
Can call the emergency number and give an address
Knows what an AED is and where to find one
Can place someone in the recovery position (certified course)
Can coordinate a simulated emergency response

items.subject: recognising-danger
items.title: Spot the danger
items.summary: Some things can hurt us. Let us find them and say STOP.
steps: 🔥 Hot things: oven, kettle, fire. Say STOP.
🔌 Plugs and wires: do not touch. Say STOP.
🚗 Roads: hold a grown-up's hand.
💊 Medicines and cleaning bottles: only grown-ups touch them.
🔪 Sharp things: knives and scissors stay with grown-ups.
👀 Point to one danger at home with your grown-up.

sources.title: Home safety
sources.publisher: Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents

check.question: A cup of tea is steaming. What do you do?
options: Stay away and tell a grown-up
check.explain: Yes. Hot drinks can burn. Stay away and tell a grown-up.

items.adultNote: Walk round your home together and name dangers calmly. Keep it a game, not a scare. Store medicines and cleaners up high and locked.

items.subject: recognising-danger
items.title: Keep yourself safe first
items.summary: If someone is hurt, stay safe first. Then get help.
steps: 🛑 Stop. Do not run in.
👀 Look. Is there fire, water, a road or wires?
🙋 Get a grown-up.
📞 No grown-up? Call your emergency number.
💛 You helped by staying safe.

check.question: Your friend is hurt in the road. What do you do first?
check.explain: Well done. Stay safe, then get help. If you get hurt too, nobody can help.

items.adultNote: This is the rule 'Do not become the second victim'. Praise the child for stopping and fetching help; that is the right action at this age.

items.subject: emergency-communication
items.title: Find a safe grown-up
items.summary: When something is wrong, find a grown-up you trust.
steps: 👨‍👩‍👧 Name your safe grown-ups at home.
🏫 Name a safe grown-up at school or nursery.
🏪 Lost in a shop? Find a person at the till or a parent with children.
🗣️ Say: I need help, someone is hurt.
🎭 Practise saying it with your grown-up.

safety.notes: Talking and role-play only.

items.adultNote: Help the child name two or three trusted adults. Practise a short clear sentence they can say under stress.

items.subject: emergency-communication
items.title: My emergency number
items.summary: Learn the number to call when someone is very hurt, and say where you live.
steps: 🔢 Learn your emergency number with your grown-up.
🏠 Learn your address: street, number, town.
🧸 Practise on a toy phone or a paper phone.
🗣️ Say: My name is ... I live at ... Someone is hurt.
👂 Listen and do what the helper says.
🚫 Only call the real number when someone really needs help.

safety.notes: Practise on a toy or pretend phone only. Do not dial the real number for practice.

check.question: When do we call the emergency number?
options: When someone is very hurt or in danger
check.explain: Yes. The emergency number is for real emergencies only.

items.adultNote: The app shows your country's number from its emergency number list; check it is right for where you live. Show how to unlock the phone or make an emergency call from the lock screen.

items.subject: hygiene
items.title: Super clean hands
items.summary: Clean hands keep germs away. Wash for as long as two birthday songs.
steps: 💧 Wet your hands.
🧼 Add soap.
👐 Rub palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs and nails.
🎵 Sing Happy Birthday two times.
💧 Rinse.
🧻 Dry with a clean towel.

safety.notes: Use cool or warm water, never hot. Wipe up splashes so nobody slips.

basic.description: Wash with soap and water from a tap or jug.

better.description: Each child has their own towel.

advanced.description: Use a sand timer or song timer for 20 seconds.

substitutions.use: a jug of clean water poured by a grown-up over a bowl
air drying with clean hands held up

items.certificationNote: Knowledge only. This app never certifies first aid. To practise and be assessed, join an accredited local first-aid course run by a qualified instructor, for example through your national Red Cross or Red Crescent society.
items.adultNote: Wash hands before and after helping with any cut or graze. Model it yourself.

items.subject: minor-cuts
items.title: Ouch! A little cut
items.summary: A small cut? Tell a grown-up. They help clean it and put on a plaster.
steps: 🙋 Tell a grown-up.
🧼 The grown-up washes hands.
💧 Rinse the cut with clean water.
🧻 Pat dry with something clean.
🩹 Put on a plaster.
🤗 Well done for being brave.

safety.notes: A grown-up cleans the cut. Practise on a teddy or a pretend cut drawn with a pen. Big or deep cuts need a doctor.

basic.description: Draw a pretend cut on a teddy and practise the steps.

better.description: Practise putting a plaster on a teddy or your own hand.

advanced.description: Look inside a real first-aid kit with your grown-up.

substitutions.use: a clean folded cloth held on by a grown-up
a pen mark on a teddy or doll

items.certificationNote: Knowledge only. This app never certifies first aid. To practise and be assessed, join an accredited local first-aid course run by a qualified instructor, for example through your national Red Cross or Red Crescent society.
items.adultNote: Get medical help if a cut is deep, gaping, will not stop bleeding with pressure, or was caused by a dirty or rusty object or an animal bite.

items.subject: burns-awareness
items.title: Hot means stop
items.summary: Hot things can burn. If you get a burn, tell a grown-up and cool it with water.
steps: ☕ Hot drinks, ovens, irons and fires can burn.
🛑 Stay back from hot things.
🙋 Burned? Tell a grown-up straight away.
💧 Cool water runs on the burn for a long time.
🚫 No butter, no ice, no cream.

check.question: What is good for a burn?
check.explain: Yes. Cool running water helps a burn. Butter and ice do not.

items.adultNote: Cool a burn under cool or lukewarm running water for about 20 minutes, remove clothing or jewellery near it unless stuck, then cover loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy cloth. Seek medical help for any burn on a young child that is bigger than a small coin or blisters.

items.subject: falls
items.title: After a fall
items.summary: If you or someone falls, stop, check, and tell a grown-up.
steps: 🛑 Stop and breathe.
🤔 Does anything hurt?
🙋 Tell a grown-up.
🧍 If someone else falls and is hurt, do not pull them up.
📞 They will not wake up? Get a grown-up or call your emergency number.
items.adultNote: After a head bump watch for drowsiness, vomiting, confusion or unusual behaviour and seek urgent medical help if they appear.

items.subject: emergency-communication
items.title: A grown-up fell and will not wake up
items.summary: A pretend story. Grandpa fell down and will not wake up. What do you do?
steps: Read the story with your grown-up.
Choose what to do at each step.
Talk about how you felt.

safety.notes: Story and role-play only.

simulation.scenario: You are at home with Grandpa. He falls down and lies still. You say his name but he does not wake up.

steps.prompt: 🛑 What do you do first?

options.text: Look around. Is it safe for me?
options.feedback: Yes. Stay safe first.
It is okay to feel scared. Stay and get help.

steps.prompt: 🙋 Is there another grown-up at home?

options.feedback: Good. A grown-up can help.
Shout loudly. Help needs to hear you.

steps.prompt: 📞 Nobody else is home. What now?

options.feedback: Yes. That is the right thing to do.
Grandpa needs help now. Call your emergency number.

steps.prompt: 🗣️ The helper on the phone asks where you live.

options.feedback: Well done. Now help can find you.
Stay on the phone. The helper needs your address.

steps.prompt: 👂 The helper tells you what to do.

options.text: Listen and do what they say
options.feedback: Great. You are a real helper.
Keep the phone with you and listen.

items.adultNote: Keep it gentle. Afterwards, practise your address and the emergency number. Tell the child that calling for help is always the right thing.

items.subject: burns
items.title: A burn from hot water
items.summary: A pretend story. Hot water spilled on a hand. What helps?
steps: Read the story.
Pick an answer at each step.
Talk about the 20 minute rule.

safety.notes: Story only. Never practise with hot water.

simulation.scenario: Your brother knocks over a cup of hot water. It splashes on his hand. He is crying.

steps.prompt: What do you do first?

options.feedback: Yes. Get a grown-up straight away.
Butter keeps the heat in. Use cool water.

steps.prompt: What helps the burn?

options.feedback: Yes. Cool or lukewarm running water for about 20 minutes.
Ice can hurt skin more. Use cool running water.
Cooling helps a lot. Use cool running water.

steps.prompt: How long should the water run?

options.feedback: Yes. A long time. A song timer helps.
Longer is better. About 20 minutes.

steps.prompt: After cooling, what covers the burn?

options.text: Cling film or a clean non-fluffy cloth, put on loosely
options.feedback: Good. It keeps it clean.
Fluffy things stick. Use cling film or a clean smooth cloth.

steps.prompt: The burn is big or blistering. What now?

options.text: A grown-up gets a doctor or calls the emergency number
options.feedback: Yes. Big burns need a doctor.
Never pop blisters. Get a doctor.

items.adultNote: For a child, seek medical help for any burn larger than a small coin, any blistering, or burns on the face, hands, feet or genitals. Call the emergency number for large or deep burns.

items.subject: scene-safety
items.title: Is it safe to help?
items.summary: Before you help, look for danger. Keep yourself safe so you do not get hurt too.
steps: 🛑 Stop before you go near.
👀 Look for traffic, fire, smoke, water, electricity, broken glass or angry animals.
👂 Listen for warnings.
🚫 If it is not safe, stay back and call for help.
✅ If it is safe, go near carefully.
🧤 Use gloves or a plastic bag on your hands if there is blood.

check.question: A person is lying near a fallen electric cable. What do you do?
options: Stay away and call the emergency number
check.explain: Right. Electricity can hurt you too. Stay away and call for help.

items.adultNote: Do not become the second victim. Children should never enter water, fire, smoke or traffic to help.

items.subject: emergency-communication
items.title: Making the emergency call
items.summary: Know what to say when you call for an ambulance, fire or police.
steps: Call your emergency number.
Say which service: ambulance, fire or police.
Say where you are: address, or landmarks you can see.
Say what happened and how many people are hurt.
Answer the questions. Stay calm and speak slowly.
Do not hang up until they tell you to.
Role-play the call with a grown-up using a pretend phone.

safety.notes: Role-play only on a pretend or switched-off phone.

items.adultNote: Many phones can call the emergency number from the lock screen. Show your child how on your phone. Some countries also accept text messages to emergency services; check locally.

items.subject: emergency-communication
items.title: The emergency call
items.summary: A pretend call. Choose the best thing to say.
steps: Read each question from the call helper.
Pick the best answer.
Practise saying your address out loud.

safety.notes: Pretend call only.

simulation.scenario: Your neighbour has fallen off a ladder and is not moving. You call the emergency number.

steps.prompt: The helper asks: Which service do you need?

options.feedback: Yes. Someone is hurt, so ask for an ambulance.
Stay on the line. Say ambulance.

steps.prompt: Where are you?

options.text: Say the address, or what you can see nearby
options.feedback: Great. Landmarks help if you do not know the address.
The helper cannot see you. Say the address or nearby landmarks.

steps.prompt: What happened?

options.text: He fell off a ladder and is not moving
options.feedback: Clear and short. Well done.
It is okay to feel upset. Take a breath and say what happened.

steps.prompt: The helper says: Stay on the line.

options.feedback: Yes. They may tell you how to help.

options.text: Hang up to call a friend
options.feedback: Stay on the line until they say you can go.

items.subject: wound-care
items.title: Clean and cover a graze
items.summary: Learn how to clean and cover a small cut or graze.
steps: Wash your hands. Wear gloves if you have them.
Press with a clean cloth if it is bleeding.
Rinse under clean running water.
Pat dry with a clean cloth.
Cover with a plaster or a clean dressing.
Tell a grown-up, and get help if it is deep, dirty or will not stop bleeding.

safety.notes: Practise on a pretend graze drawn on a friend or doll. Real wounds are cleaned with a grown-up.

basic.description: Draw a pretend graze and practise the steps.

better.description: Practise putting on plasters and a small gauze pad.

advanced.description: Practise with gloves and a full first-aid kit.

substitutions.use: a clean plastic bag over each hand
a clean, ironed cotton cloth

items.certificationNote: Knowledge only. This app never certifies first aid. To practise and be assessed, join an accredited local first-aid course run by a qualified instructor, for example through your national Red Cross or Red Crescent society.

items.subject: bleeding
items.title: Press to stop bleeding
items.summary: Firm pressure on a wound helps stop bleeding.
steps: Check it is safe. Put on gloves or plastic bags.
Press firmly on the wound with a clean pad or cloth.
Keep pressing. Do not keep lifting to look.
If blood comes through, add another pad on top and keep pressing.
Get a grown-up. Call the emergency number if the bleeding is heavy.
Practise tying a bandage on a partner's arm (not too tight).

safety.notes: Practise bandaging on each other only with a grown-up watching. Check fingers stay pink and warm. Never use real blood.

basic.description: Practise pressure and a scarf bandage on a partner's arm.

better.description: Practise with a real roller bandage.

advanced.description: Practise a full dressing with gloves from a first-aid kit.

substitutions.use: a long strip of clean cotton cloth or a scarf
clean plastic bags over the hands

items.certificationNote: Knowledge only. This app never certifies first aid. To practise and be assessed, join an accredited local first-aid course run by a qualified instructor, for example through your national Red Cross or Red Crescent society.
items.adultNote: Do not remove anything stuck in a wound; press around it and get medical help.

items.subject: burns
items.title: Burns: cool, call, cover
items.summary: Cool a burn under cool running water for about 20 minutes, get help, then cover it loosely.
steps: Make sure the danger is gone (turn off heat if safe, or move away).
Cool the burn under cool or lukewarm running water for about 20 minutes.
Take off rings, watches or clothes near the burn unless they are stuck.
Get a grown-up. Big or deep burns need the emergency number.
Cover loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy cloth.
No ice, butter, toothpaste or creams. Never pop blisters.

check.question: How long should you cool a burn?
check.explain: Yes. About 20 minutes of cool running water.

items.certificationNote: Knowledge only. This app never certifies first aid. To practise and be assessed, join an accredited local first-aid course run by a qualified instructor, for example through your national Red Cross or Red Crescent society.

items.subject: nosebleeds
items.title: Nosebleed? Lean forward
items.summary: Sit down, lean forward and pinch the soft part of your nose.
steps: Sit down.
Lean forward, not back.
Pinch the soft part of the nose, just below the bony bit.
Breathe through your mouth.
Keep pinching for 10 to 15 minutes. Use a clock.
Spit out any blood in your mouth rather than swallowing it.
Tell a grown-up. Get medical help if it is still bleeding after 10 to 15 minutes of pinching, it is very heavy, it makes breathing hard, or it came after a hard bump to the head.

safety.notes: Practise the position without a real nosebleed. A grown-up helps with a real one.

basic.description: Practise sitting, leaning forward and pinching for one minute.

better.description: Add tissues and a timer to your practice.

advanced.description: Pack tissues and a cold pack in a first-aid kit.

substitutions.use: counting slowly or singing songs
a clean cloth

items.certificationNote: Knowledge only. This app never certifies first aid. To practise and be assessed, join an accredited local first-aid course run by a qualified instructor, for example through your national Red Cross or Red Crescent society.

items.subject: nosebleeds
items.title: Nosebleed at playtime
items.summary: A pretend story. Your friend has a nosebleed. Help them.
steps: Read the story.
Pick the best answer.
Show the nosebleed position.

safety.notes: Story only.

simulation.scenario: At playtime your friend's nose starts to bleed. They look worried.

steps.prompt: What do you say first?

options.text: Let's tell a teacher. Sit down here.
options.feedback: Yes. Calm words and a grown-up help.
Be kind. Help them sit and get a grown-up.

steps.prompt: How should they sit?

options.feedback: Yes. Leaning forward stops blood going down the throat.
Tipping back sends blood down the throat. Lean forward.

steps.prompt: Which part of the nose do they pinch?

options.feedback: Yes. Just below the bony bit.
Pinch the soft part lower down.

steps.prompt: It is still bleeding after 15 minutes of pinching.

options.feedback: Yes. Long nosebleeds need a doctor or nurse.
A long nosebleed needs a grown-up to get medical help.

items.subject: sprains
items.title: Twisted ankle
items.summary: Rest, cool, support and raise a sprained ankle or wrist.
steps: Stop playing and rest.
Cool it: a cold pack wrapped in a cloth for up to 20 minutes.
Support it with a soft bandage, not too tight.
Raise it on a cushion.
Get it checked if you cannot stand on it, it looks the wrong shape, or it is very painful.

safety.notes: Practise bandaging a partner with a grown-up watching. Never put ice straight on skin.

materials: bag of frozen peas wrapped in a towel

better.description: Practise a figure-of-eight ankle bandage on a partner.

advanced.description: Practise a wrist support and a sling.

substitutions.use: a bag of frozen vegetables wrapped in a tea towel
a long scarf

items.certificationNote: Knowledge only. This app never certifies first aid. To practise and be assessed, join an accredited local first-aid course run by a qualified instructor, for example through your national Red Cross or Red Crescent society.

items.subject: fractures
items.title: Could it be broken?
items.summary: Learn the signs of a broken bone and how to keep it still until help comes.
steps: Signs: bad pain, swelling, the wrong shape, cannot move it.
Keep the person still and calm.
Support the injured part in the position you find it. Do not try to straighten it.
Get a grown-up and medical help. Call the emergency number for a leg, neck, back or a bone through the skin.
Do not move someone who may have hurt their neck or back unless they are in danger.
items.certificationNote: Knowledge only. This app never certifies first aid. To practise and be assessed, join an accredited local first-aid course run by a qualified instructor, for example through your national Red Cross or Red Crescent society.

items.subject: choking
items.title: Spot choking
items.summary: Choking means food or an object blocks the airway. Spot it and get help fast.
steps: Signs: cannot talk, cannot breathe, holds the throat, face changes colour.
If they can cough, tell them: keep coughing!
If they cannot cough or breathe, shout for a grown-up NOW.
No grown-up? Call your emergency number.
Eat sitting down and chew well to help prevent choking.

check.question: Your friend is coughing hard on food but can still cough. What do you say?
check.explain: Yes. Coughing is the best way to clear it. Get a grown-up if the coughing stops working.

items.certificationNote: This app teaches knowledge and never certifies. Hands-on skills such as CPR, choking response, AED use and the recovery position must be learned and assessed with a qualified instructor at an accredited local first-aid course (for example through your national Red Cross or Red Crescent society or a resuscitation council approved provider).

items.subject: fainting
items.title: Feeling faint
items.summary: Fainting is a short loss of consciousness. Lying down with legs raised usually helps.
steps: Signs before fainting: dizzy, pale, sweaty, blurry eyes.
Feeling faint? Sit or lie down straight away.
If someone faints: check it is safe, help them lie on their back.
Raise their legs on a bag or cushion.
Give them air. When they feel better, sit up slowly.
If they do not wake up within a minute or so, call the emergency number.
items.certificationNote: Knowledge only. This app never certifies first aid. To practise and be assessed, join an accredited local first-aid course run by a qualified instructor, for example through your national Red Cross or Red Crescent society.

items.subject: seizures
items.title: Helping during a seizure
items.summary: During a seizure: protect them, time it, do not hold them down, and never put anything in their mouth.
steps: Stay calm. Check it is safe and move hard or sharp things away. Only move the person if they are in danger.
Cushion their head with something soft.
Time the seizure.
Do not hold them down. Do not put anything in their mouth.
When the jerking stops, put them on their side in the recovery position (or help a grown-up do it) and stay with them, talking calmly, until they are fully awake.

Call the emergency number if it lasts more than 5 minutes, it is their first seizure, another seizure starts, they are injured, have trouble breathing, the seizure happened in water, or they do not wake up.

check.question: Which of these is right during a seizure?
options: Put a spoon in their mouth
Time it and protect their head
check.explain: Yes. Protect, time it, and never restrain or put anything in the mouth.

items.certificationNote: This app teaches knowledge and never certifies. Hands-on skills such as CPR, choking response, AED use and the recovery position must be learned and assessed with a qualified instructor at an accredited local first-aid course (for example through your national Red Cross or Red Crescent society or a resuscitation council approved provider).
items.adultNote: If the person has an epilepsy care plan, follow it. Treat with dignity: give space and privacy.

items.subject: allergies
items.title: Allergic reactions
items.summary: Some people are allergic to foods, stings or medicines. A bad reaction is an emergency.
steps: Know if you or a friend has an allergy.
Mild signs: itchy rash, sneezing, runny eyes.
Emergency signs: swelling of lips or tongue, trouble breathing, wheezing, feeling faint.
Emergency signs? Get a grown-up and call the emergency number straight away.
Some people carry an adrenaline pen (auto-injector). If they have one, they or a grown-up use it straight away.
Never share food with someone who has a food allergy unless their grown-up says it is safe.
items.certificationNote: Knowledge only. This app never certifies first aid. To practise and be assessed, join an accredited local first-aid course run by a qualified instructor, for example through your national Red Cross or Red Crescent society.

items.subject: heat-illness
items.title: Hot days and drinking water
items.summary: On hot days drink water, find shade and rest. Know the signs of getting too hot.
steps: Drink water often, even before you feel thirsty.
Wear a hat and play in the shade.
Signs of too much heat: headache, dizzy, tired, very thirsty, dark pee.
Feeling like this? Stop, go somewhere cool, drink water and tell a grown-up.
If someone is confused, has a fit, faints, is not sweating even though they are very hot, or still feels unwell after 30 minutes resting somewhere cool, a grown-up calls the emergency number.
items.certificationNote: Knowledge only. This app never certifies first aid. To practise and be assessed, join an accredited local first-aid course run by a qualified instructor, for example through your national Red Cross or Red Crescent society.

items.subject: poisoning
items.title: Poison: do not touch
items.summary: Medicines, cleaners, some plants and berries can poison. Do not touch, taste or sniff them.
steps: Only take medicine from a trusted grown-up.
Never drink from unlabelled bottles.
Do not eat wild berries or mushrooms unless a grown-up who knows says it is safe.
If someone swallowed something harmful: tell a grown-up straight away and keep the container.
Do not make them sick. A grown-up calls the emergency number or poison advice line.

sources.title: Home safety
sources.publisher: Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents

items.adultNote: Find your local poison information number and keep it with your emergency numbers.

items.subject: first-aid-kit
items.title: Build a first-aid kit
items.summary: Make a simple kit and learn what each thing is for.
steps: Find a clean box or bag.
Add plasters, gauze pads, a bandage, tape, gloves and scissors with round ends.
Add a list of emergency numbers and your address.
A grown-up adds any medicines and keeps them out of reach.
Label the box with the first-aid sign: a white cross on a green background. (The red cross is a protected emblem, so do not use it.)
Check it every few months and replace used things.

safety.notes: Use round-ended scissors. Medicines are chosen and stored by an adult only.

basic.description: A box with clean cloths, plastic bags for gloves and a list of numbers.

better.description: A basic kit with plasters and dressings.

advanced.description: A full kit with gloves and a foil blanket.

substitutions.use: a clean shoe box or zip bag
clean plastic bags

items.certificationNote: Knowledge only. This app never certifies first aid. To practise and be assessed, join an accredited local first-aid course run by a qualified instructor, for example through your national Red Cross or Red Crescent society.

items.subject: cpr
items.title: What is CPR?
items.summary: CPR helps when someone's heart stops. You can learn what it is now, and do a real course when you are older.
steps: The heart pumps blood around the body.
If someone collapses and is not breathing normally, their heart may have stopped.
First: get a grown-up and call the emergency number. The call helper will guide you.
CPR means pushing hard and fast on the middle of the chest to keep blood moving.
A machine called an AED can help restart the heart. It talks and tells you what to do.
Real CPR is learned on a training doll in a class with a qualified instructor.
items.certificationNote: This app teaches knowledge and never certifies. Hands-on skills such as CPR, choking response, AED use and the recovery position must be learned and assessed with a qualified instructor at an accredited local first-aid course (for example through your national Red Cross or Red Crescent society or a resuscitation council approved provider).
items.adultNote: Never let children practise chest compressions on a person. Many schools and Red Cross or Red Crescent societies run courses for young people.

items.subject: primary-assessment
items.title: Primary assessment: DRSABCD
items.summary: A simple order to check someone who is hurt or unwell: Danger, Response, Send for help, Airway, Breathing, CPR, Defibrillation.
steps: D - Danger: check it is safe for you, bystanders and the casualty.
R - Response: speak loudly and tap their shoulders. Do they answer or open their eyes?
S - Send for help: call the emergency number (on speaker) or get someone else to.
A - Airway: open the airway by gently tilting the head back and lifting the chin.
B - Breathing: look, listen and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds.
C - CPR: if not breathing normally, start CPR (hands-only if untrained) and follow the call helper.
D - Defibrillation: send someone for an AED, switch it on and follow its prompts.
Some countries teach DR ABC or the primary survey; the order of priorities is the same.

check.question: What does the first D stand for?
check.explain: Danger. Always check your own safety first.

items.subject: recovery-position
items.title: Recovery position (practice)
items.summary: The recovery position keeps the airway open for someone who is breathing but not responding.
steps: Use only for someone breathing normally but not responding, with no suspected spinal injury.
Kneel beside them. Place the near arm at a right angle.
Bring their other hand across their chest and hold the back of it against the cheek nearest you.
Bend the far knee up, then roll them towards you onto their side.
Tilt the head back so the airway stays open.
Call the emergency number if not already done. Keep checking their breathing until help arrives. If breathing stops or is not normal, start CPR.
Practise slowly on a willing family member lying on a soft floor, with an adult watching.

safety.notes: Practise only on a willing partner on a soft floor with adult supervision. Roll slowly. Stop if anything hurts.

basic.description: Practise the steps slowly on a partner.

better.description: Practise with a step card and swap roles.

advanced.description: Learn and be assessed by a qualified instructor.

substitutions.use: a folded blanket or rug
a large soft toy or pillow to rehearse hand positions

items.subject: severe-bleeding
items.title: Severe bleeding
items.summary: Severe bleeding is life threatening. Call for help and apply firm direct pressure.
steps: Check for danger. Protect your hands with gloves or plastic bags.
Call the emergency number, or get someone to.
Press firmly and directly on the wound with a clean pad. Keep pressing.
If blood soaks through, add more pads on top; do not remove the first.
If something is stuck in the wound, do not pull it out; press around it.
Help them lie down and keep them warm; watch for signs of shock.
Tourniquets and wound packing are only for people trained to use them.

safety.notes: Practise pressure and bandaging on each other with adult supervision. Check circulation beyond the bandage. No real blood.

basic.description: Practise direct pressure and a scarf bandage.

advanced.description: Learn bleeding control with a qualified instructor.

substitutions.use: a clean folded cloth and a scarf
plastic bags over the hands

items.subject: shock
items.title: Recognising shock
items.summary: Shock happens when the body does not get enough blood flow, for example after heavy bleeding or burns.
steps: Signs: pale, cold, clammy skin; fast breathing; fast weak pulse; feeling sick, faint or anxious.
Call the emergency number.
Treat the cause, such as bleeding, if you can do so safely.
Help them lie down. Raise and support their legs if this does not hurt them.
Keep them warm with a coat or blanket and reassure them.
Do not give food or drink. Keep checking breathing and response.

items.subject: cpr
items.title: Hands-only CPR
items.summary: If an adult collapses and is not breathing normally, call for help and push hard and fast in the centre of the chest.
steps: Check for danger and response. Shout for help.
Call the emergency number on speaker. Send someone for an AED.
Kneel beside them. Put the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, other hand on top.
With straight arms, push down about 5 to 6 cm, then let the chest come fully back up.
Push 100 to 120 times a minute (about two a second). Some people use the beat of a fast song.
As soon as an AED arrives, switch it on and follow its voice prompts, keeping pauses in CPR as short as possible.
Keep going until help takes over, the AED tells you to stop, the person starts breathing normally, or you are too exhausted. Swap with another helper every 2 minutes if you can.

Untrained bystanders give hands-only CPR. Trained responders may add rescue breaths (30 compressions to 2 breaths), especially for children and drowning. For a child, still call and start CPR: the call helper will guide you.
PRACTICE: only on a training manikin with a qualified instructor. Never push on a real person's chest for practice.

hazards: chest injury if practised on a person
safety.notes: Compressions are practised only on a CPR training manikin under a qualified instructor. At home, rehearse hand position and rhythm on a firm cushion only.

basic.description: Rehearse hand position and the 100-120 rhythm on a firm cushion only.

better.description: Join a free community CPR awareness session if available.

advanced.description: Learn and be assessed on a manikin with a qualified instructor.

substitutions.use: a firm cushion for hand-position and rhythm practice only (never compress on a person)
counting out loud, or a song with about 100-120 beats per minute

items.subject: aed
items.title: Find the AED
items.summary: An AED (defibrillator) gives an electric shock that can help a heart get back to a normal beat. It talks you through every step. Learn where they are.
steps: Look for the green or white heart-with-lightning sign in shops, stations, schools and sports centres.
Note where the nearest AEDs are to your home and school.
In an emergency, send someone to fetch it while CPR continues.
Switch it on and follow the voice prompts. Stick the pads on the bare chest where the pictures show.
Stand clear when it says, then continue CPR when told.
Hands-on practice uses a training AED with a qualified instructor.

hazards: electric shock from a real device
safety.notes: Never handle a real AED for practice. Practise only with a training AED (no shock) under a qualified instructor. Walking to find AED locations is fine.

basic.description: Walk your area and map the AED locations.

materials: online video from a resuscitation council
better.description: Watch an official AED demonstration video together.

advanced.description: Practise with a training AED and a qualified instructor.

substitutions.use: a cardboard box with drawn pad pictures to rehearse the steps (no device)

items.subject: choking
items.title: Choking response (adult)
items.summary: Know the steps to help a choking adult or child over 1 year. Practise movements only with an instructor.
steps: Ask: Are you choking? If they can cough, encourage them to keep coughing.
If they cannot cough, speak or breathe: shout for help and get someone to call the emergency number.
Give up to 5 sharp back blows between the shoulder blades, with them leaning forward.

If that does not work, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts: stand behind them, put a fist between the belly button and the bottom of the breastbone, hold it with your other hand and pull sharply inwards and upwards.
If it still has not cleared, call the emergency number if not already done, and keep alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until help arrives.
If they become unresponsive, call for help and start CPR.
Anyone given abdominal thrusts should be checked by a doctor afterwards.
Never practise back blows or abdominal thrusts on a real person. Use a manikin with an instructor.

hazards: internal injury if practised on a person
safety.notes: Practise the hand positions in the air only. Real practice needs a choking training manikin and a qualified instructor.

basic.description: Learn the steps and rehearse hand positions in the air.

better.description: Watch an official choking video from a first-aid organisation.

advanced.description: Practise on a choking manikin with a qualified instructor.

substitutions.use: a large cushion to show hand positions only, with no force

items.subject: drowning
items.title: Drowning: reach or throw, don't go
items.summary: Never jump in to save someone. Call for help, then reach or throw something that floats.
steps: Shout for help and call the emergency number. At a beach or pool, alert the lifeguard.
Stay on land. Lie down so you are not pulled in.
Reach with a stick, pole, towel or clothing.
Throw something that floats: a ring, ball, bottle or cool box.
Tell them to kick and hold on. Keep watching where they are.
Once they are out and safe, if they are not breathing normally, start CPR. Trained responders give rescue breaths first for drowning.
Anyone rescued from water should see a doctor, even if they seem fine.

items.subject: temperature-emergencies
items.title: Too hot, too cold
items.summary: Heatstroke and hypothermia are emergencies. Learn the signs and first steps.
steps: Heat exhaustion: headache, dizziness, heavy sweating, cramps, feeling sick. Move to a cool place, lie down, raise feet, sip water, cool the skin. If they are not better within 30 minutes, treat it as heatstroke.

Heatstroke: very hot skin (they may stop sweating), confusion, fits or collapse. Call the emergency number and cool them quickly with cool water and fanning while you wait. If they become unresponsive but are breathing, put them in the recovery position.
Hypothermia: shivering, pale cold skin, slow speech, confusion, sleepiness.
For hypothermia: get to shelter, replace wet clothes, wrap in blankets including the head, give a warm (non-alcoholic) drink if fully alert.
Hypothermia is an emergency: call the emergency number. Handle them gently. Do not rub limbs, use a hot bath or very hot water, or give alcohol.

items.subject: allergies
items.title: Anaphylaxis and auto-injectors
items.summary: Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction. Call the emergency number and help the person use their adrenaline auto-injector.
steps: Signs: swelling of throat or tongue, trouble breathing or swallowing, wheeze, pale or floppy, collapse.
Help them use their own adrenaline auto-injector into the outer thigh straight away, following the instructions on it.
Call the emergency number and say anaphylaxis, even if they start to feel better.
Lie them down with legs raised. If breathing is hard, let them sit up. Do not let them stand up or walk.
A second dose may be given after 5 minutes if there is no improvement and they have one.
If they stop breathing normally, start CPR.
Practise only with a needle-free trainer pen.

hazards: needle injury from a real auto-injector
safety.notes: Never practise with a real auto-injector. Use a needle-free trainer pen with an adult. Real devices belong to the person prescribed them.

materials: trainer pen from a family member's prescription pack
better.description: Practise with a needle-free trainer pen.

advanced.description: Practise allergy response on a course with an instructor.

substitutions.use: a marker pen with its cap on to rehearse the hold and thigh position

items.subject: diabetic-emergencies
items.title: Diabetic emergencies
items.summary: People with diabetes can have very low blood sugar. Know the signs and how to help.
steps: Low blood sugar signs: shaky, sweaty, pale, confused, irritable, hungry.
If they are awake and can swallow: give a sugary drink, glucose tablets or sweets. Wait 10 to 15 minutes; if they are not better, give more sugar. Once they recover, give something starchy.
Help them check their blood sugar if they have a meter.
If they do not improve after two sugar treatments, get worse, become drowsy or unresponsive: do not give anything by mouth. Call the emergency number.
If unresponsive and breathing, a trained person places them in the recovery position.

items.subject: triage
items.title: More than one casualty: triage
items.summary: When several people are hurt, triage helps decide who needs help first.
steps: Your safety first. Do not enter a dangerous scene.
Call the emergency number. Say how many people are hurt.
Quickly check each person. The quiet ones may be the most serious.
Highest priority: not breathing normally, or bleeding heavily.
People who can walk and talk are usually lower priority; ask them to help or wait in a safe place.
Hand over clearly to the emergency services and follow their instructions.

items.subject: primary-assessment
items.title: Someone has collapsed
items.summary: A simulated emergency. Make safe choices step by step.
steps: Read the scenario.
Choose an action at each step.
Review the feedback and the DRSABCD order.

safety.notes: Decision-making simulation only. Do not act it out with real compressions.

simulation.scenario: Walking past a bus stop, you see an adult suddenly collapse to the ground. Nobody else is helping yet.

steps.prompt: What do you do first?

options.text: Check the scene is safe: traffic, hazards, falling objects
options.feedback: Correct. Danger first so you do not become the second victim.
Never put yourself in danger. Check the scene first.

options.text: Walk on, someone else will help
options.feedback: Your help matters. Check the scene is safe, then act.

steps.prompt: It is safe. How do you check responsiveness?

options.text: Shout 'Can you hear me?' and tap their shoulders
options.feedback: Correct. A loud voice and a gentle tap.
Shaking could cause injury. Tap shoulders and speak loudly.
That can block the airway. Speak loudly and tap shoulders.

steps.prompt: No response. What next?

options.text: Shout for help and call the emergency number on speaker
options.feedback: Correct. Get help coming early. The call helper can guide you.

options.text: Wait a few minutes to see if they wake up
options.feedback: Every minute counts. Call now.
Never give anything by mouth to someone who is not responding.

steps.prompt: You open the airway (tilt head, lift chin) and check breathing for up to 10 seconds. They are only gasping occasionally.

options.text: Treat it as not breathing normally: start hands-only CPR and send someone for an AED
options.feedback: Correct. Occasional gasps are not normal breathing.
Gasps can happen in cardiac arrest. Start CPR.

options.text: Put them in the recovery position and leave
options.feedback: Recovery position is for someone breathing normally. Start CPR.

steps.prompt: How do you do hands-only CPR?

options.text: Centre of the chest, about 5-6 cm deep, 100-120 per minute, full recoil
options.feedback: Correct. Hard and fast in the centre of the chest.
Compressions go in the centre of the chest, hard and fast.

options.text: Slow, one press every few seconds
options.feedback: Aim for 100-120 compressions per minute.

steps.prompt: Someone arrives with an AED.

options.text: Switch it on and follow the voice prompts; keep CPR going until it says stand clear
options.feedback: Correct. The AED guides you. Minimise pauses in CPR.

options.text: Do not touch it, only doctors can use it
options.feedback: AEDs are designed for the public. Switch it on and follow the prompts.

steps.prompt: What if they had been breathing normally but not responding?

options.text: Keep the airway open (recovery position if trained), keep checking breathing, wait with them for help
options.feedback: Correct. Monitor them until help arrives.

options.text: Sit them up and give food
options.feedback: Never give food or drink. Keep the airway open and monitor.

items.subject: choking
items.title: Choking at dinner
items.summary: A simulated emergency. An adult at dinner is choking.
steps: Read the scenario.
Choose an action at each step.
Talk about why each step comes in that order.

safety.notes: Decision-making only. Never practise back blows or abdominal thrusts on a person.

simulation.scenario: At a family dinner, your uncle suddenly stops eating, grabs his throat and looks panicked.

steps.prompt: What do you do first?

options.text: Ask: Are you choking? Can you cough?
options.feedback: Correct. Find out if the airway is partly or fully blocked.

options.text: Slap his back straight away without asking
options.feedback: First check if he can cough. Coughing is most effective if possible.

steps.prompt: He is coughing strongly.

options.text: Encourage him to keep coughing and stay with him
options.feedback: Correct. A strong cough may clear it.
Do not give drinks. Encourage coughing.

steps.prompt: Now he cannot cough, speak or breathe.

options.text: Shout for someone to call the emergency number, then give up to 5 back blows
options.feedback: Correct. Get help coming and start back blows.
A full blockage is life threatening. Act now.

steps.prompt: Back blows have not worked.

options.text: Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts, then keep alternating with back blows
options.feedback: Correct. Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until it clears or help arrives. The call helper can guide you.

options.text: Put fingers blindly down his throat
options.feedback: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper.

steps.prompt: He becomes unresponsive.

options.text: Make sure the emergency number has been called and start CPR
options.feedback: Correct. CPR can also help move the blockage.

options.text: Keep doing back blows on the floor
options.feedback: If unresponsive, start CPR and follow the call helper.
